title: Why Sweden raised rates with CPIF inflation still at 1.5%
summary: The Riksbank announced a 25-basis-point increase to 2% on 4 November with Swedish inflation below target. Its case rested on what could happen as the economy recovered. A weaker krona and renewed supply disruptions had raised costs, while stronger demand could make it easier for firms to pass those costs on. The Board expected both headline and underlying inflation to rise above 2% in 2027. September’s forecast had already envisaged tightening. Further increases over the coming year were likely only if the outlook for inflation and activity continued to hold.

The inflation figures in the opening paragraphs explain why September’s 1.5% CPIF reading had limited bearing on the decision by itself. Temporary fiscal measures were holding down measured prices. Removing their direct effect put inflation at 3%. Removing energy as well gave 1.6%, the measure the Riksbank judged most informative about underlying pressure at the time. Headline inflation matched the forecast, while the 1.6% measure came in slightly below it. The difference between the two adjusted readings shows how sensitive the comparison was to energy. The 3% figure alone would overstate the evidence of a broad increase in persistent inflation.

The forward-looking case for tightening came from the combination of demand and costs. Disruption associated with the war in the Middle East was still affecting supply, energy prices had increased further and inflation abroad had risen. The weaker krona during the year added a potential source of imported price pressure. Cost indicators were above normal even as the preferred underlying price measure surprised on the low side. A rise in what firms pay for inputs reaches consumer prices only to the extent that firms pass it on. The Board’s expectation of a stronger economy helps explain why those cost indicators mattered for next year.

Preliminary third-quarter GDP and employment had both increased in line with forecast. In October firms became more optimistic while households became less so. The Board expected activity to reach normal levels in 2027 and labour-market conditions to improve, though the strength of that improvement remained uncertain. Its risk discussion allows for two different global effects. Continuing disruption could make prices higher even as geopolitical uncertainty, concerns over AI investment or weak public finances abroad weighed on demand. A faster Swedish recovery would strengthen the inflation case. Weak household demand would make pass-through less assured.

The increase took effect on 11 November. The communiqué scheduled a press conference for 11:00 on the announcement day and the minutes for 10 November. The accompanying Monetary Policy Update assessed new information without publishing a new forecast. The next scheduled forecast was on 16 December. For interest-rate investors, the November message concerned the Board’s continued confidence in September’s path. There is no market pricing in the communiqué from which to infer how much of that guidance investors had anticipated.

questions.question: What would establish that the projected rise in underlying inflation was taking hold?
questions.detail: The 3% figure excludes temporary fiscal measures but still includes energy. The preferred underlying reading was 1.6% and slightly below forecast. Reconcile all three readings with the official CPIF component weights and the September forecast vintage, then examine monthly changes in non-energy goods and services. The breadth and persistence of those moves would affect how much additional tightening a short-rate investor might expect.

questions.question: Was demand strong enough for firms to pass on higher costs?
questions.detail: Preliminary activity and employment broadly matched the forecast, yet firms and households reported opposite changes in sentiment. Compare firms’ selling-price plans and orders with official household consumption and labour-market data available around the meeting. Distinguish firms exposed to imported energy or inputs from those selling domestic services. Absorbing costs in margins would have different implications for both the policy path and corporate earnings than a broad rise in final prices.

questions.question: Which part of the expected rate path changed on the announcement?
questions.detail: The Board tied further hikes to September’s conditional outlook. Compare SEK overnight-indexed swap rates spanning the November decision with contracts covering later 2027 meetings, using quotes before the announcement and before the 11:00 press conference. Examine the minutes separately when released. A move further out the curve could reflect a change in expected policy duration even if investors had priced the 25-basis-point increase in full.
